t.6.56.1: Seeing Kumbhakarṇa slain by the great-souled Rāghava, the rākṣasas reported it to Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas.
t.6.56.2: Hearing that the mighty Kumbhakarṇa had been slain in battle, Rāvaṇa, burning with grief, swooned and fell down.
t.6.56.3: Hearing that their paternal uncle had been slain, Devāntaka and Narāntaka, Triśiras and Atikāya wept, tormented by grief.
t.6.56.4: Hearing that their brother had been slain by Rāma, whose deeds are performed without strain, Mahodara and Mahāpārśva were overcome with grief.
t.6.56.5: Then, having regained consciousness with difficulty, that bull among rākṣasas, Rāvaṇa, wretched because of the slaying of Kumbhakarṇa, lamented.
t.6.56.6: Alas, O hero, crusher of the pride of foes, O mighty Kumbhakarṇa! Having single-handedly scorched the enemy host, where are you going, abandoning me?
t.6.56.7: Now indeed I am no more, I whose right arm has fallen, the arm relying on which I feared neither the gods nor the asuras.
t.6.56.8: How could such a hero, the crusher of the pride of gods and Dānavas, the very likeness of the fire of universal destruction, have been slain today in battle by Rāghava?
t.6.56.9: You, whom even the crushing blow of the thunderbolt could never bring to harm, how is it that you now lie asleep upon the surface of the earth, stricken by Rāma's arrows?
t.6.56.10: These hosts of gods, standing in the sky together with the sages, seeing you slain in battle, roar with delight.
t.6.56.11: Surely this very day the monkeys, thrilled at having found their target, will scale the fortified gates of Laṅkā here on every side.
t.6.56.12: I have no use for the kingdom; what shall I do with Sītā? Bereft of Kumbhakarṇa, I take no delight in life.
t.6.56.13: If I do not slay in battle Rāghava, the slayer of my brother, then surely death is better for me, and not this futile life.
t.6.56.14: This very day I shall go to that place where my younger brother is, for I cannot bear to live even for a moment having abandoned my brothers.
t.6.56.15: The gods will surely laugh when they see me, who once did them wrong. How shall I conquer Indra, O Kumbhakarṇa, now that you are slain?
t.6.56.16: So now the auspicious counsel of Vibhīṣaṇa has come home to me, the counsel of that great-souled one which, out of ignorance, I did not accept.
t.6.56.17: Vibhīṣaṇa's words have proved true, for this dreadful destruction of Kumbhakarṇa and Prahasta that has come to pass fills me with shame.
t.6.56.18: This morning has come to me the grief-bringing fruit of that deed of mine, namely that the righteous and glorious Vibhīṣaṇa was cast out by me.
t.6.56.19: Thus, his inmost soul in turmoil, having lamented Kumbhakarṇa piteously and in many ways, Daśānana, sorely afflicted, then fell to the ground, knowing that his younger brother, the foe of Indra, had been slain.
